author: JIM FRANZ
title: Beloit's Darren Coleman to break into pro MMA ranks - NewsBreak
text: BELOIT — Darren Coleman attended his 10-year reunion Saturday, having graduated from Beloit Memorial High School in 2015. When it comes to “what are you doing lately?” conversations, he no doubt shocked many of his former classmates. At 28, Darren “The Kobra” Coleman will debut as a pro Mixed Martial Arts fighter on Saturday in Shakopee, Minn., at the Canterbury Park Expo Center. “I think that caught a lot of people I went to school with off guard,” he said. “In high school, I was somewhat athletic, but I was always the skinny guy and never the strongest guy. The only sports I did was freshman wrestling for a month or two and after winning a couple of matches I competed in a tournament and got destroyed. So I quit.” Coleman said watching a Youtube video of MMA fighters training led to an epiphany in his 20s. “I watched the video and thought, man, this looks interesting,” he said. “It sounds crazy, but that night I had a dream about working out in a gym and fighting. When I woke up I had the motivation to go out and do it.” The 6-foot-1 Coleman was hooked as soon as he stepped into the gym. Even if it didn’t go the way he initially expected. “The first day at the gym it was spar day and I didn’t let anybody know about it, but I had to go to the doctor because I injured my jaw,” he said. “I went back, though. It’s always good to know how to defend yourself whether you have aspirations of becoming an MMA fighter or not. At first, I didn’t think I was going to go on and fight at this level. I just wanted to get in shape and learn self-defense. But then I started improving and doing well against the people in the gym who were better than me at the start. I found out I can take a punch in the face.” That was when he was around 23, rather a late start for an MMA fighter. That didn’t dissuade him from trying to make up for lost time by quickly starting his amateur career. He has trained at Janesville’s Fearless MMA gym for about five years now with Patrick Delgado as his trainer. “I got into the deep end pretty quick,” he says with a chuckle. “I decided to get into actual competitions and one match kept leading to one more. I fought three or four times right away and none of the matches lasted more than a minute and 40 seconds. They were knockouts or submissions. I became the No. 1 amateur featherweight in Wisconsin in less than a year and won the Chosen Few belt as well, which at the time was the No. 1 promotion in Wisconsin. He said he “walks around at 160 pounds,” but will get down to 145 to fight in the Featherweight division where he is ranked No. 1 in Wisconsin. He has also fought at 155 in the Lightweight division and is ranked No. 3 in that division in Wisconsin. “I’m still not a heavy guy, but I added 30 or 40 pounds of muscle from my high school days,” he said. “Believe me, I like donuts and hotdogs, but when I need to cut weight and go into fight camp, my body is used to it.” Of his six amateur wins, two are by knockouts, one by TKO and three by submission. His only loss in seven amateur fights was to Tres Leon, a four-time NAIA All-American wrestler, on April 13, 2024. That was his second amateur fight. “I had tried wrestling as a kid and I was trash,” he said. “I fought him early in my career and I didn’t know much about wrestling. It was a five-round fight for a title. He had only lost one wrestling match his whole career and he was wrestling heavy. I was getting up and I was rocking him at times, but I couldn’t finish.” The match went the full five rounds and finally to the judges with Coleman losing by an unanimous decision. “To go five rounds with a wrestler of that magnitude was a plus for me,” he said. “I have a hard roster of fights as an amateur. Three different promoters told me they were having a hard time lining up opponents to face me because no one wanted to. I had the No. 1 guy in Illinois lined up and the day of the fight he pulled out of it. “So I was having trouble finding fights and I think with a 6-1 record, I’d done everything I needed to do. I was sparring with pros who were excelling as pros. So I thought it was time for me to turn pro. I know this is a hard journey, but I want to see if I have what it takes.” In Minnesota, he will fight 26-year-old Dylan Smerillo out of Mound, Minn., in Ignite Fights 109. Smerillo has a pro record of 2-3-0. “He is a real scrappy guy who likes to brawl,” Coleman said. “He is pretty good at striking. Like I said, they always throw me in the deep end. I’m going pro so they get me a veteran in his hometown so I’m going to be the guy getting booed. But it makes you feel that much better when you pull off the upset and bring the victory back to Beloit.” He even plans on bringing a city flag into the cage with him in Minnesota. “I’m proud to have Beloit on my back,” he said. “Proud to represent where I come from. All the support I get all around me really motivates me and keeps me going.” He has higher hopes than winning in Shakopee. “This has really become a lifestyle for me,” he said. “I’m in the gym every day and I really want to be a UFC champion, honestly. It sounds crazy. There was a time when I just wanted to be champion of Wisconsin. My confidence keeps rising. I want to put myself in the position where I can not only help my wife and kids, but also help the other people around me. I want to help motivate people in my hometown, young and old. I never saw myself doing that, but now I feel like I have more of a purpose.” • NOTES: The fight is available from the streaming service at spectationsports.com. …Coleman is thankful he has some outstanding sponsors, including Martindale Pinnacle Construction, Simmons Fence and Specialty Products, Your Pretty Dope and Dr. Dunlap’s Ink Therapy.
